insight.title: You Are Living Through the Shortest Era of History
insight.subtitle: Why the speed of modern change makes the past look like a flat line.
insight.notificationHook: History is moving faster than you think.

sections.text: Most of what you recognize as human history was essentially static. For thousands of years, the tools, light sources, and travel speeds available to a person in 1000 BC were nearly identical to those in 1700 AD.

Then, you arrived. In the blink of a single lifetime, the pace of transformation has accelerated so violently that the last century contains more technological upheaval than the previous ten millennia combined.
We tend to view the timeline as a steady progression of centuries, but we are currently occupying a frantic, outlier spike that bears no resemblance to the quiet, predictable pace of our ancestors.
The past was a long plateau; you are in the vertical climb.

audioBrief.script:
Welcome to your Sift Daily Briefing. Here is the clear, plain version of today's news.

Next, Democrats took control of the United States Congress after winning sweeping midterm elections. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries is in line to become the first Black speaker in January. He promised swift action on living costs and the war in Iran within one hundred hours. His priorities include reversing nearly one trillion dollars in Medicaid cuts made under President Donald Trump. Representative Robert Garcia, who expects to chair the House Oversight Committee, told Republicans to lawyer up. Democrats can now use committees to demand documents, summon officials, and start investigations. Trump praised Democrats after the election and said he expected to work with them on immigration. However, Trump previously warned that he would veto every bill if Democrats won Congress.

Turning to energy news, oil prices fell and then recovered during trading on Monday. Brent crude initially fell more than six point five percent to one hundred five dollars and fifty-five cents. That was its lowest price since October sixteenth. The price dropped because people hoped the United States and Iran would end their war. Prices later regained some losses after new United States military strikes hit targets in Iran. Iran says talks with Qatari mediators about reopening the Strait of Hormuz are still continuing. The Iranian Foreign Minister stated that those talks have not produced an agreement yet.

In technology and finance, large American tech companies are borrowing heavily to build artificial intelligence systems. Four major companies have sold about two hundred fifty billion dollars in bonds since early twenty twenty-five. Those companies are Amazon, Google owner Alphabet, Meta, and Oracle. Microsoft also recently sold twenty-five billion dollars in bonds. Goldman Sachs projects total new AI bond sales will reach four hundred twenty billion dollars next year. This heavy borrowing forces European countries and businesses to compete for the same investment funds. French ten-year bond yields climbed from about three point seven percent to nearly five percent recently. French interest payments are set to reach ninety-one billion euros next year.

Moving to corporate news, Meta is raising fifteen billion dollars by selling new bonds. Meta is the parent company that owns Facebook. The company plans to use the money to build artificial intelligence infrastructure and data centers. This bond sale includes three point two five billion dollars due in twenty thirty-one. It also includes three point two five billion dollars due in twenty thirty-three. Meta previously raised twenty-five billion dollars through a bond sale in April. Meta expects capital spending between one hundred thirty-five billion and one hundred forty-five billion dollars this year. Moody's assigned the new debt an Aa3 rating. Meta had eighty-three point six seven billion dollars in total debt on September thirtieth.

In cryptocurrency news, a major security breach hit the exchange company Binance last week. Chief Executive Officer Richard Teng told CNBC that Binance restored ninety-eight percent of affected customer assets. The total value of affected assets was six point three four billion dollars. Other companies including Tether, Circle, and Ripple froze about three billion dollars in stolen assets. Coinbase also blocked transfers to compromised wallets and offered direct assistance to Binance. ClearStreet analyst Owen Lau says larger companies have more resources to invest in cybersecurity. Morgan Stanley analyst Felix Stratmann says repeated breaches could encourage investors to move assets to independent custodians.

Finally, Cyprus is expanding military cooperation with the United States after decades of close ties with Russia. United States Ambassador John Breslow announced plans to upgrade an air base in Paphos, Cyprus. The upgrades will allow the base to host large American military transport aircraft. Breslow also announced more frequent visits by United States warships to Cypriot ports. He assured a local news agency that the United States will protect Cyprus in the future. Cyprus originally maintained a non-aligned foreign policy after gaining independence from the United Kingdom in nineteen sixty. University of Nicosia professor Konstantinos Adamides said Russia's twenty twenty-two invasion of Ukraine triggered the shift. He noted that Cyprus openly chose to side with the West despite the economic costs.

Up next, Google plans to invest fifteen billion dollars in Malaysia during twenty twenty-seven and twenty twenty-eight.

Google will invest fifteen billion dollars in Malaysia from 2027 to 2028. The spending goes towards data centre campuses, clean energy, water security and upskilling workers, according to Alphabet, the parent company of Google. Google plans to build new campuses in Selangor and Negeri Sembilan. The construction phase is expected to contribute an annual average of one billion one hundred million dollars to Malaysia's GDP. The facilities once operational are projected to sustain more than 9,000 local jobs per year. Google also plans to add more than one gigawatt of clean energy capacity to the national grid.

Five global banks have set up a Singapore-based non-profit organisation to boost infrastructure for tokenised financial markets. Called the Global Layer One Organisation, the initiative brings together HSBC, Kinexys by JPMorgan, MUFG, Societe Generale-Forge and Standard Chartered. The banks announced the move in a joint release on Wednesday. The organisation builds on the Monetary Authority of Singapore initiative that explores shared ledger infrastructure. The framework helps regulated financial institutions deploy tokenised assets across jurisdictions.

America's renters are increasingly missing payments and turning to costly short-term credit. The Federal Reserve reports that more than one in eight renters were at least sixty days late on a loan payment in the past year. Since 2019, rents in America have risen by forty-two percent, while renters' household incomes went up by thirty-four percent. The typical renter has just two thousand dollars in liquid savings, compared to twelve thousand dollars for mortgage-holders. More than one in ten renters took out a payday loan or paycheque advance in 2025.

Colombia's Congress passed a bill toughening terms for members of illegal armed groups who hand themselves in. President Abelardo De La Espriella proposed the bill, which breaks with the total peace policy of former president Gustavo Petro. The Senate approved the bill with fifty-seven votes in favour versus twenty-four against. The House of Representatives backed it by ninety-five votes to ten on Tuesday. The number of armed group members in Colombia grew from 15,120 at the end of 2022 to approximately 28,802 in July 2026. Under the new bill, leaders cannot receive sentences of less than ten years.

Canva announced job cuts and a sweeping overhaul that impacts twenty-two percent of its workforce. Chief executive officer Melanie Perkins said that 1,271 people will lose their jobs, change roles or relocate to central hubs. Canva is an online design and publishing platform based in Sydney. Perkins co-founded the company with Cliff Obrecht and Cameron Adams. Canva's valuation tumbled to roughly twenty-six billion dollars in 2022 after hitting a forty billion dollar high in 2021.

Taliban officials have been invited to attend an upcoming United Nations climate summit as observers. The summit starts next week in Antalya in Turkey. Rohullah Amin, head of climate change at Afghanistan's environment protection agency, confirmed that Kabul plans to attend. The United Nations has not allowed the Taliban to take up Afghanistan's seat at the General Assembly. Afghanistan is one of the countries most vulnerable to climate change, facing a compounding crisis of drought and extreme heat.

Before we go, here is your thought for the day.

Most of what we call human history was essentially static. For thousands of years, the tools and travel speeds of a person in 1000 BC were nearly identical to those in 1700 AD. In the blink of a single lifetime, the pace of transformation has accelerated so violently that the last century contains more technological upheaval than the previous ten millennia combined. We tend to view the timeline as a steady progression of centuries. Instead, we are occupying a frantic spike that bears no resemblance to the predictable pace of our ancestors. The past was a long plateau, and we are in the vertical climb. How do you adapt when your entire world changes faster than history ever moved before?

Thanks for listening to this edition of the Sift Daily Briefing.

audioBriefIndepth.script:
Welcome to your Sift In-Depth Briefing. This is our full analysis of three major global stories.

Could Democrats taking control of the US Congress change how the country is run? Yes, their victory gives them power to block Donald Trump, investigate his government, and stop his nominees. Voters were upset about high living costs, fuel prices, and the war in Iran. So they voted for change in the midterm elections. Midterm elections are votes held midway through a president's four-year term. 

To understand how we got here, we have to look back at American politics. Donald Trump won the presidency again for a second term. His Republican Party had controlled both houses of Congress. Congress is the American lawmaking body, made up of two parts: the House of Representatives and the Senate. During the first half of Trump's term, his party passed his plans. But voters grew frustrated over high prices and military actions. 

Then the election changed the balance of power. Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress. That outcome makes them the majority party in the House and the Senate. Because of that win, the opposition party now holds the tools to challenge the president. 

Today, the news is all about what Democrats plan to do with their new power. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries is in line to become the speaker, which is the leader of the House. He promised a major push in the first one hundred hours of the new Congress. Democrats want to lower living costs, restore health insurance subsidies, and reverse nearly one trillion dollars in Medicaid cuts. Medicaid is a government health program for poor people. They also plan to roll back tariffs, which are taxes on imported goods. On the oversight side, lawmakers are preparing investigations. Oversight means watching over the government to catch corruption. Robert Garcia, a Democrat expected to head the House Oversight Committee, told Republicans to lawyer up. Oregon Senator Ron Wyden posted a single word: subpoenas. A subpoena is a legal order requiring someone to hand over documents or testify. Democrats might investigate family business dealings, cryptocurrency, and government contracts involving billionaire Elon Musk. They also control confirmations, meaning they can block cabinet and judicial nominees. 

Why is this happening right now? The timing comes straight from the midterm election cycle, which ended with voters expressing deep frustration over the economy and the war in Iran. 

What does this mean for you, and what should you watch next? Trump still holds the presidential veto, which lets him reject laws passed by Congress. Overriding a veto takes a two-thirds vote in both chambers, which is very hard to reach. Watch whether Democrats actually force a government shutdown over spending battles, or if both sides find ways to compromise. 

Moving from Washington to the global energy markets, why did oil prices drop to a four-week low? Oil prices eased because investors hoped peace talks might end wars, even as recent attacks threatened supplies. 

The story of oil prices is tied to conflicts around the world. Russia invaded Ukraine in twenty twenty-two, which caused western nations to place sanctions on Russian energy. Sanctions are official penalties that stop trade. At the same time, the United States and Iran have been locked in a long-running conflict. These wars disrupted oil supplies and sent fuel costs soaring. 

Then a new diplomatic push changed the mood. Qatar stepped up mediation efforts between the US and Iran. Qatar is a small middle eastern country that often acts as a neutral go-between. At the same time, Russia confirmed it will hold peace talks with Ukraine and the US in Abu Dhabi. 

Today, the market is reacting to a mix of peace hopes and ongoing violence. Brent futures fell one dollar and seventeen cents to settle at one hundred three dollars and sixty dollars a barrel. US West Texas Intermediate crude fell thirty-seven cents to settle at ninety-six dollars and nine cents. A senior Iranian official told Reuters that Iran and the US are still far from a deal. Overnight, the US carried out strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island. A US official said the strikes targeted surface-to-air missiles. In Russia, a Ukrainian drone attack set fire to a major oil refinery in the city of Yaroslavl. Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia is working to expand a pipeline to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. That strait is a narrow water channel that once carried twenty percent of global oil supplies. 

Why is this happening at this moment? Qatar is pushing for a deal right after the US midterm elections, while military commanders on both sides keep launching sudden strikes. 

What does this mean for the listener? If peace talks succeed, oil prices could fall further, bringing relief to drivers. But if the fighting worsens, fuel costs could spike again. Watch for the weekly US storage reports from the American Petroleum Institute and the Energy Information Administration to see if crude stockpiles are growing. 

Finally, could the AI boom make borrowing more expensive in Europe? Yes, because US tech giants are borrowing massive amounts of money, which drives up interest rates for everyone else. 

To see how this started, look at the artificial intelligence buildout. Building AI requires huge computer centers and vast amounts of money. Big tech companies began pouring more than one trillion dollars into this technology. Four of the biggest firms, known as hyperscalers—Amazon, Google owner Alphabet, Meta, and Oracle—started borrowing heavily. They issued about two hundred fifty billion dollars in US bonds and thirty-seven billion euros in Europe. Bonds are loans that investors buy, which pay regular interest over time. 

Then Microsoft joined the borrowing spree with a twenty-five billion dollar bond sale. Goldman Sachs projects that total new AI bond sales will reach four hundred twenty billion dollars next year. 

Today, that massive borrowing is hitting European markets. Viktor Hjort of BNP Paribas calls this "bond abundance," which creates fierce competition for available investment funds. That competition is bad news for European countries like France, Germany, and Italy, whose sovereign bond yields have risen sharply. Sovereign bonds are loans issued by governments. France is already paying a high risk premium because its public debt is one hundred nineteen percent of its gross domestic product, which measures the total value of goods and services produced. Yields on French ten-year bonds climbed from roughly three point seven percent to nearly five percent. The French interest bill is set to rise from seventy-nine billion euros to ninety-one billion euros next year. The European Central Bank warned that these giant tech debts could make it harder for other companies and governments to access finance. 

Why is this happening right now? Tech companies need cash immediately to fund their AI data centers, coinciding with a moment when European governments are already struggling with high public debt and rising energy prices. 

What does this mean for Europe? European companies may have to cut investments in new plants and research to pay off expensive loans. Taxpayers could end up paying more on government debt, partly to finance an AI boom happening across the Atlantic. Watch whether European central banks take steps to protect local borrowers from being priced out by American tech giants. 

Next up, we look at how Meta raised fifteen billion dollars in a five-part US bond sale to fund its AI expansion.

How is Meta paying for its massive new push into artificial intelligence? The Facebook parent company is raising fifteen billion dollars through a five-part US bond sale. 

Long ago, Meta mostly relied on the cash it earned from ads to grow. But building artificial intelligence requires giant data centres and powerful computers. Because that equipment costs huge amounts of money, Meta started borrowing. In April, Meta sold twenty-five billion dollars in bonds. Last year, the company sold thirty billion dollars in bonds. 

Then things changed. Meta revealed that its full-year capital spending will reach up to one hundred forty-five billion dollars, driven by artificial intelligence. That is a five billion dollar increase to the low end of its previous guidance. 

Now, on Tuesday, Meta announced a fifteen billion dollar debt sale in five parts. One part is three point twenty-five billion dollars in notes due in 2031 with a five point eighty-five percent coupon. Another part is three point twenty-five billion dollars due in 2033 at six point twenty-five percent. This follows a move to expand plans for what could become a ninety-seven point five billion dollar equity raise. 

This happens right now because the race for artificial intelligence infrastructure demands more cash than cash balances can provide. S&P Global Ratings revised Meta's outlook to negative, citing uncertainty over this heavy spending and negative free cash flow of two point twelve billion dollars for the latest quarter. 

For the listener, this means big tech firms are taking on heavy debt to fund new technology. Moody's assigned the new debt an Aa3 rating, expecting Meta to maintain conservative financial policies. You might want to watch whether this giant debt load pays off with profitable artificial intelligence tools.

How can investors keep digital money safe after a massive cyber attack? The six point three billion dollar Binance hack is pushing the crypto industry to focus heavily on custody providers and security infrastructure. 

For years, crypto companies focused mostly on trading volume and transaction fees. But last Thursday, a breach hit Binance, the world's largest centralized cryptocurrency exchange. This combined trading, custody, and settlement all in one place, creating big risks. 

Then things changed when Binance got hacked. Unlike the FTX leadership fraud in late 2022, Binance leadership moved fast to protect customers. 

Today, Binance CEO Richard Teng told CNBC that the company has replenished ninety-eight percent of the six point thirty-four billion dollar affected assets. Other firms helped freeze about three billion dollars in stolen assets. Now, analysts say the industry must separate custody from execution so independent banks and vaults hold the coins while exchanges handle the trades. 

This happens now because institutional investors want to adopt digital assets, but they demand proof that funds are safe under extreme pressure. 

For the listener, this points to a shift where security matters more than just user numbers. You might want to watch whether independent custodians gain market share as investors demand safer storage.

Why is Cyprus shifting its foreign policy away from Russia and toward the United States? The new United States ambassador to Cyprus announced plans to upgrade a major air base and expand joint military activities. 

After gaining independence from Britain in 1960, Cyprus kept a neutral stance. Under its first president, Archbishop Makarios III, Cyprus joined the Non-Aligned Movement to avoid taking sides between the United States and the Soviet Union. Later, a 1974 Turkish invasion created deep anger toward the United States, which backed Turkey as a NATO ally. Because the United States imposed an arms embargo on Cyprus in 1987, the Cypriot military relied on Russian weapons and signed naval agreements with Moscow. 

Then things changed in February 2022 when Russia invaded Ukraine. Cyprus chose to join European Union sanctions against Russia despite the economic cost to its tourism and services. 

Today, US Ambassador John Breslow told the Cyprus News Agency that the United States will protect Cyprus in the future. The United States also suspended its old arms embargo, and Cyprus is now working to phase out Russian weapons like T-80 tanks and Buk air defense systems. 

This happens now because the 2022 war in Ukraine broke decades of Cypriot neutrality and proved to Washington that Nicosia is a reliable partner in the Eastern Mediterranean. 

For the listener, this shows how a nation can pivot its alliances during global conflicts. You might want to watch if Cyprus can eventually join NATO despite opposition from Turkey.

That leads into our next story about how Google plans to invest fifteen billion dollars in Malaysia in 2027 and 2028.

Why is Google spending 15 billion U.S. dollars in Malaysia?
The company is building new data centers to expand its computer network across Southeast Asia.

To understand this move, we have to look at how the internet works.
When you search online or stream a video, computers process that data somewhere.
Those computers live inside large facilities called data centers.
Data centers require a lot of electrical power to run continuously.
They also need water to keep hot computer equipment cool.
For a long time, tech companies kept most of their servers in Western nations.
Over time, millions of new internet users came online across Southeast Asia.
Tech firms needed to build facilities closer to these new users.
Malaysia became a popular choice for these building projects.
The country offered available land, growing power grids, and a central location in the region.
Google already built its first Malaysian data center campus at Elmina Business Park in Selangor state.
That initial campus is already up and running today.

Now, Google is taking its commitment in Malaysia to a larger level.
The tech company has announced plans for a large investment starting in 2027.

Google says it will invest 15 billion U.S. dollars in Malaysia in 2027 and 2028.
The money comes from Alphabet, which is the parent company of Google.
Ruth Porat is the president and chief investment officer of Alphabet and Google.
She says the spending matches Malaysia's national development priorities.
The investment will cover new data center campuses, clean energy, water security, and job training.
Google plans to build new campuses in Selangor state and Negeri Sembilan state.
During construction, Google says the project will add 1.1 billion U.S. dollars annually to Malaysia's economy.
That building work will support more than 37,000 local jobs each year.
Once the sites open, they are projected to sustain over 9,000 local jobs annually.
Those jobs will pay wages averaging 45 percent above the national median income.

Why is this investment happening right now?
Google says it needs foundational computing capacity to support digital innovation across the country.
As its operations scale up, the company must also secure more local power and water resources.

This project could help Malaysia build up its digital infrastructure over the coming years.
Google plans to add more than one gigawatt of clean energy capacity to the national grid.
The company promises to pay for 100 percent of the power its campuses use.
It will also pay direct infrastructure costs to connect its sites to the grid.
Google says the sites will run efficiently, with a power usage effectiveness between 1.12 and 1.14.
It also announced four new programs to upskill 800,000 Malaysians over five years.

Now let us move from tech investments to changes in global banking.

Why are five of the world's top banks joining forces in Singapore?
They are launching a non-profit group to create shared standards for digital financial markets.

To understand this move, we need to look at how money and investments are changing.
Banks are exploring a technology called tokenisation.
Tokenisation turns traditional financial assets, like bonds or money, into digital tokens on a shared ledger.
A shared ledger is a secure digital record book shared across a computer network.
Tokenisation can make trading faster, cheaper, and more connected across borders.
However, different banks and technology companies started building their own separate digital systems.
When systems cannot talk to each other, trading across different platforms becomes very difficult.
To help solve this, the Monetary Authority of Singapore created an initiative called GL1.
The Monetary Authority of Singapore is Singapore's central bank and financial regulator.
The GL1 project explored how regulated institutions could safely deploy digital assets.
It developed control rules to check if digital market systems were safe and reliable.
It also created ways to build policy and legal requirements directly into digital networks.

Now, the banks are expanding this work into a permanent, independent organization.
Five global banking leaders have set up a new non-profit group based in Singapore.

The new initiative is called the Global Layer One Organisation, or GL1 Org.
The five founding members are HSBC, Kinexys by JPMorgan, MUFG, Societe Generale-Forge, and Standard Chartered.
Ruby Ho is managing director and head of markets and securities services for Asean at HSBC.
She says tokenisation makes markets faster and more connected, but clients must trust the underlying infrastructure.
Patrick Lee is chief executive officer for Singapore and Asean and South Asia at Standard Chartered.
He says common policy and market standards are critical for digital assets to work together globally.
GL1 Org will advance shared frameworks so institutions can operate across different networks with confidence.

Why is this happening right now?
Tokenisation is gaining momentum around the world.
As various digital market infrastructures emerge, banks need common rules so different systems can connect.

This initiative could help build a trusted, connected digital foundation for global finance.
The organization says it welcomes participation from banks, policymakers, market providers, and fintech firms across jurisdictions.
By setting clear standards, the group hopes to support further scaling of digital financial infrastructure.

Next, we turn to the financial struggles facing millions of households in the United States.

Why are renters in the United States facing serious financial trouble today?
A growing financial gap is leaving tenants far behind homeowners despite overall economic growth.

To understand this divide, we have to look back at past economic shocks.
During the global financial crisis of 2007 to 2009, homeowners suffered the most.
By 2010, one in 20 mortgages was in foreclosure.
One in ten mortgage holders was delinquent on payments.
House prices fell by nearly a quarter during that crisis.
Nearly one in four homeowners owed more than their home was worth.
In recent years, the overall U.S. economy began growing steadily again.
That growth was boosted by artificial intelligence investments and strong consumer spending.
However, over the past three or four years, a clear divide opened up.
Renters now make up about one third of all American households.
While homeowners remained financially resilient, tenants began struggling much more with rising living costs.

An analysis by The Economist shows that renters are increasingly missing payments.
Data shows tenants are turning to high-cost short-term credit to cover basic monthly living expenses.

The Federal Reserve published its latest Survey of Consumer Finances last month.
The Federal Reserve is the central bank of the United States.
More than one in eight renters was at least 60 days late on a loan payment.
That is the highest rate since records began in 1989.
Another Fed survey from late 2025 found a quarter of renters missed bill payments.
By comparison, only one in ten mortgage holders missed bill payments.
About one in six renters finds it difficult to get by.
Demographics explain part of this gap, as renters tend to be younger and earn less.
In 2025, median household income was 57,000 dollars for renters, versus 103,000 dollars for homeowners.
Our analysis shows demographic factors explain only three-fifths of the gap between renters and homeowners.
One real example is Jacob Ramirez, an operations manager for a café chain in California.
He accumulated 28,000 dollars in credit card debt to cover expenses and rent.
He is now working with a non-profit debt counseling service to pay that off by 2028.

Why is this happening right now?
Since 2019, U.S. rents rose 42 percent while renters' household incomes rose only 34 percent.
When leases expire, renters face higher payments whether they can afford them or not.
Also, the typical renter has only 2,000 dollars in liquid savings, compared to 12,000 dollars for homeowners.
Ted Gayer of the JPMorgan Chase Institute says many homeowners support spending by withdrawing brokerage funds.
The restart of student loan repayments after the pandemic also added heavy financial strain.
That restart accounted for about half of the recent rise in renters falling behind on debts.

This widening gap means millions of renters are taking on high-cost short-term loans.
Data shows renters are now more likely than mortgage holders to incur late credit card fees.
More than one in ten renters took out a payday loan or paycheck advance in 2025.
Whitney Airgood-Obrycki of Harvard University's Joint Centre for Housing Studies says higher rents make saving harder.
Without savings, tenants may struggle to prepare for emergencies or buy their own homes.

Next, Colombia's congress has passed a bill replacing a former president's total peace approach.

Why is Colombia changing how it deals with armed illegal groups? Lawmakers in Colombia just voted to replace the government's old peace policy with much tougher rules.

For six decades, Colombia suffered through a deadly internal conflict between the government and illegal armed groups. That long conflict killed more than four hundred fifty thousand people over sixty years. In late twenty twenty-two, Colombia's first leftist president, Gustavo Petro, took office. Petro was a former member of a guerrilla group called M nineteen. He started an ambitious plan called total peace to end the fighting. He restarted peace negotiations with a group called the National Liberation Army. Petro also suspended arrest warrants for fighters and agreed to ceasefires. However, those peace talks produced very few tangible results. The Ministry of Defense reported that armed groups actually grew larger during this period. At the end of twenty twenty-two, illegal armed groups had fifteen thousand one hundred twenty members. By July twenty twenty-six, that number grew to approximately twenty-eight thousand eight hundred two members. Critics argued that Petro's peace negotiations allowed armed groups to expand into drug trafficking and illegal mining. Towards the end of his term, Petro acknowledged that total peace was not fully achieved. But he pointed out that homicides across Colombia had reduced under his plan. Then, a right-wing leader named Abelardo De La Espriella ran for president. During his campaign, he promised to end peace talks with leftist guerrillas and criminal gangs. He pledged to deploy the military against those groups instead.

President De La Espriella proposed a new bill that breaks directly with Petro's total peace policy.

Colombia's Congress has now passed De La Espriella's bill in sessions that ended late on Tuesday. The Senate approved the measure with fifty-seven votes in favor and twenty-four against. The House of Representatives supported it ninety-five to ten. The new legislation bars members of illegal armed groups from holding public office. It also prevents them from entering into future peace negotiations with the government. To receive reduced prison sentences, fighters must meet a series of strict conditions. They must lay down their weapons and identify fellow group members. They must hand over recruited and kidnapped minors. They must contribute to the search for missing people and surrender their assets. They must also provide information about political ties and corruption networks. In exchange, prison sentences can be reduced by up to fifty percent. Group commanders can receive a sentence reduction of up to thirty percent. Leaders cannot receive sentences shorter than ten years. Crucially, the bill does not suspend arrest warrants, extradition, or law enforcement operations.

The right-wing president wants to deliver on his key election promise right away.

Now, the legislation goes to President De La Espriella to be signed into law. This victory could mark a permanent shift away from government peace talks with armed groups. However, it is possible that military operations will lead to renewed clashes across the country.

Now, turning to business news, artificial intelligence is reshaping another prominent technology company.

Why is the online design platform Canva cutting so many jobs? Chief Executive Officer Melanie Perkins announced job cuts because artificial intelligence is changing how software is built.

Canva is a popular online design and publishing platform based in Sydney, Australia. It was co-founded thirteen years ago by Melanie Perkins, Cliff Obrecht, and Cameron Adams. For a decade, Canva grew rapidly without slowing down. In twenty twenty-one, private investors valued the company at forty billion U.S. dollars. But a year later, a tech selloff knocked Canva's valuation down to roughly twenty-six billion dollars. While its valuation later rebounded, new industry troubles soon emerged. Artificial intelligence programs like Claude, made by Anthropic PBC, began doing tasks that required specialty software. This technology allows people to create designs easily on their own. At the same time, companies are using artificial intelligence to operate with fewer employees. Investors worry that AI will take business away from traditional software companies. As a result, investors wiped billions of dollars from the value of software firms. Growth at Canva slowed for the first time in a decade, prompting its leadership to act.

Perkins decided that small adjustments would no longer protect the business from these structural changes.

On Wednesday, Canva announced an overhaul affecting about twenty-two percent of its workforce. A total of one thousand two hundred seventy-one people will lose jobs, change roles, or relocate. Perkins broke the news in a note posted to the firm's website. She wrote that new technology is transforming what people create and what they expect from products. She added that small changes would not be enough. Perkins described this reorganization as the hardest moment in Canva's thirteen-year history. Under the new plan, Canva will return to running small, empowered teams with fewer niche specializations. Sydney will become the primary base for more product teams. Most hybrid staff will spend two to three days a week in the office starting in January.

Canva is preparing for a potential stock market listing, making financial balance critical.

The overhaul leaves Canva balancing its finances carefully as tech markets remain unpredictable. Meanwhile, investors wonder if huge investments in artificial intelligence will actually produce financial returns. Other Australian tech companies are feeling the strain. Data center firm Firmus Grid recently canceled a planned stock listing of up to five point five billion U.S. dollars. Data center operator Nextdc also saw its shares plummet in October after cutting earnings guidance. Analysts will watch closely to see if Canva's restructuring stabilizes its business before going public.

Next, global climate talks are bringing a controversial ruling group back to the international stage.

Why are Taliban officials attending the upcoming United Nations climate summit? Representatives from Afghanistan were invited as observers because their country is facing severe environmental disasters.

The Taliban returned to power in Afghanistan in twenty twenty-one as U.S.-led military forces pulled out. They established government rules based on their strict interpretation of Islamic law. Dissent is not tolerated, and protests against government decisions are illegal. The Taliban implemented severe restrictions on women, including a ban on girls' education beyond the sixth grade. They also limited what women can wear and where they can go. Because of these harsh policies, most United Nations member states do not formally recognize the Taliban government. The United Nations has not allowed the Taliban to take Afghanistan's seat at the General Assembly. At the same time, Afghanistan is one of the countries most vulnerable to global climate change. The country faces a compounding crisis of drought, water scarcity, extreme heat, and unpredictable flooding. Most Afghans depend heavily on agriculture, and recurring droughts have severely weakened local food production. Between April and December last year, over one point six million people left their homes in Afghanistan. The International Organization for Migration reported that climate impacts on their lives drove this massive displacement. Two years ago, Taliban officials attended a United Nations climate summit in Baku, Azerbaijan, for the first time. Since then, leadership groups of U.N. climate conferences deferred decisions on who officially represents Afghanistan. That choice largely froze Taliban leaders out of global climate talks.

Now, organizers have invited Taliban officials to attend the next global climate conference as observers once again.

The upcoming summit, officially known as COP thirty-one, starts next week in Antalya, Turkey. Rohullah Amin, head of climate change at Afghanistan's environment protection agency, confirmed Kabul plans to attend. A Turkish official, speaking on condition of anonymity, also confirmed that Afghan Taliban officials will attend. An observer can attend meetings and discussions, but has no formal role in negotiating policies or goals. Taliban officials argue that Afghan citizens must have representation and access to international climate finance. Sayedmuhammad Sulimankhil, executive director of the Kabul-based organization Samsoor Watan, agreed that climate aid should continue. He stated that the Afghan community faces climate consequences, not the government itself. However, former Afghan lawmaker and women's rights activist Fawzia Koofi strongly criticized Taliban attendance. She argued that the Taliban cannot represent a country when they exclude women and children from society.

The summit begins next week, forcing organizers to settle attendance questions for observer nations right now.

This invitation highlights the tough balance world leaders face during worsening climate crises. They want to deliver emergency aid to suffering populations without granting political legitimacy to authoritarian rulers. Observers will watch to see whether Taliban officials can build support for climate funding despite international sanctions.

Now, let us step back from today's headlines for a broader perspective on human history.

Before we go, here is your thought for the day.

Most of what you recognize as human history was essentially static. For thousands of years, basic daily life stayed almost completely unchanged. Tools and travel speeds in one thousand BC were nearly identical to those in seventeen hundred AD. Light sources used by ordinary people were also virtually the exact same. People lived in a quiet, predictable rhythm for dozens of centuries.

Then, you arrived. In the blink of a single lifetime, the pace of transformation has accelerated violently. The last century contains more technological upheaval than the previous ten millennia combined. We tend to view the timeline as a steady progression of centuries. But we are currently occupying a frantic, outlier spike. Our fast-paced world bears no resemblance to the quiet pace of our ancestors. The past was a long plateau. You are living in the vertical climb.

It is extraordinary to think about how rare our current moment truly is. We expect technological change every year. But for thousands of years, human life barely shifted across entire generations. Today, a single decade can transform how the whole world works.

When you look at your routine today, what part of modern life would surprise your ancestors the most?

Thank you for taking time to listen to Sift In-Depth today. Take care, and we will talk to you again soon.
